title: A 17-Year Study of 82,000 People Found That Ultraprocessed Food Raises Your Risk of Dying by 10 Per Cent. The Damage Starts in Childhood.
excerpt: The highest consumers also faced a 20 per cent higher risk of dying from nervous system diseases and a 28 per cent higher risk from other causes. A separate study found the cardiovascular toll begins in preschool.
body:
A study of 82,221 people followed for 17 years has found that those who ate the most ultraprocessed food had a 10 per cent higher risk of dying from any cause. The findings, published in Frontiers in Nutrition in May 2026, add to a rapidly growing body of evidence that the packaged, industrially formulated foods lining supermarket shelves are doing measurable harm — and that the damage starts in childhood.

## What the Study Found

Researchers analysed dietary data from the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial, a large US cohort. Participants reported their food intake at baseline between 1993 and 2001, and were tracked for a median of 17 years. During that period, 24,237 deaths occurred.

The results were stark. Participants in the highest quarter of ultraprocessed food consumption, compared with the lowest, had a 10 per cent higher risk of all-cause mortality, a 9 per cent higher risk of dying from circulatory diseases, a 20 per cent higher risk of dying from nervous system diseases including dementia, and a 28 per cent higher risk of dying from other causes. Ultraprocessed food intake was not associated with cancer mortality specifically, though separate studies have found links to breast cancer risk.

One finding offered a sliver of nuance. Among those with the highest ultraprocessed food intake, people who still managed to maintain a high overall diet quality — measured by the Healthy Eating Index — had significantly lower mortality risk than those who ate poorly overall. In other words, if you cannot eliminate packaged food entirely, the quality of everything else on your plate still matters.

## The Children Are Not Spared

A separate study published in Contemporary Pediatrics in May 2026 tracked more than 1,400 preschool-aged children for up to 10 years through the Childhood Obesity Risk Assessment Longitudinal Study. Children with the highest ultraprocessed food consumption showed increases in BMI, waist circumference, fat mass, and unfavourable changes in their lipid profiles over the follow-up period.

"Our findings give cause for concern," said principal investigator Nancy Babio of the Unit of Human Nutrition at Universitat Rovira i Virgili. "The boys and girls taking part in our study were very young but, even so, there was a significant relationship between their consumption and these parameters."

Earlier research from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children, published in JAMA Pediatrics, found similar results: children in the highest fifth of ultraprocessed food consumption gained an additional 0.20 kilograms per year and saw waist circumference increase by an extra 0.17 centimetres per year compared with those eating the least processed diets.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

South Asian families in the United States face a particular version of this problem. The shift from home-cooked dal, sabzi, and roti to packaged convenience food is not just a cultural loss — it is a measurable health risk for a population already predisposed to cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.

A 2025 Lancet Series on ultraprocessed foods documented the global displacement of traditional diets by industrially formulated products, driven by aggressive marketing and the convenience demands of dual-income households. For Indian American families, this often means children grow up on packaged cereals, flavoured yogurts, frozen meals, and sweetened beverages rather than the minimally processed foods their grandparents ate.

The irony is not lost on nutritionists who study this community. South Asians carry genetic variants that increase cardiometabolic risk at lower BMI thresholds than other populations. Adding a diet high in ultraprocessed food to that baseline creates what researchers call a compounding risk — the dietary pattern accelerates the disease trajectory that genetics has already primed.

## What You Can Do

The research does not demand perfection. The Frontiers study showed that maintaining overall diet quality can offset some of the harm from ultraprocessed food. For South Asian families, this means the dal and sabzi you cook at home is doing more work than you think. Fresh vegetables, legumes, whole grains, and home-prepared meals remain the single most effective dietary intervention available — no supplements required.

The practical advice from multiple studies converges on three points: read ingredient lists and avoid products with substances you would not use in a home kitchen, prioritise home cooking even if it means simpler meals, and pay particular attention to what children eat between meals, since snack time is where ultraprocessed food consumption concentrates most heavily.

The 82,000-person study did not set out to indict any specific product. But its 17-year follow-up period and clear dose-response relationship make the conclusion difficult to dismiss. The more ultraprocessed food you eat, the higher your risk of dying earlier. For a community already fighting elevated cardiovascular and metabolic risk, that finding is not academic. It is personal.
